title: Analysis of platelet function in patients with infection and sepsis
summary:
Sepsis is a life-threatening condition triggered by a severe infection. It leads to an excessive immune response that not only fights the infection but can also damage the body’s own tissues and organs. This may result in organ failure and, without prompt treatment, death. Platelets, also known as thrombocytes, are small blood cells primarily responsible for blood clotting. In sepsis, platelets can exhibit abnormal activation, increasing the risk of blood clots and thrombosis. At the same time, through the release of signaling molecules, they can modulate inflammatory responses in the body.

The present study investigates how platelet function and activation are altered in sepsis and the clinical significance of these changes for disease progression. The aim is to improve our understanding of the condition and to contribute to the development of future therapeutic strategies. In addition, a range of clinical data will be collected during the observation period (e.g., age, sex, comorbidities, presence of thrombosis), along with selected laboratory parameters.

interventions.name:
Patients with sepsis or septic shock and SOFA score ≥ 7
Blood samples will be collected at the following time points:
Day 1 (day of study inclusion)
Day 3
Day 7
At discharge
Optional later time point one month after discharge

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
-Age >= 18 years
-Written informed consent from the patient or their legal representative or authorized proxy
-	SOFA ≥ 7
Exclusion criteria:
Pregnancy or breastfeeding
ECMO treatment prior to study inclusion
Aplasia following chemotherapy or hematopoietic stem cell transplantation
